t.2.1: Here comes the season of clouds like a king, my beloved, blazing with fierce splendour and dear to all lovers: the spray-laden rain-clouds are its rutting elephants, the lightning its banners, and the crash of thunder its drums.
t.2.2: The sky is covered on every side with clouds: in some places they have the loveliness of deep-blue lotus petals, in others they resemble heaps of crushed collyrium, and in others they have the dark sheen of the breasts of pregnant women.
t.2.3: Implored by flocks of cātaka birds distraught with thirst, the rain-clouds, sagging under their burden of water, move slowly onward, pouring down in many streams, their thunder delightful to the ear and the heart.
t.2.4: And the clouds, their drums the crash of thunderbolts, bearing the bow of the lord of the gods strung with lightning, violently pierce the hearts of those far from home with the fierce arrows of their falling, very sharp streams of rain.
t.2.5: Strewn with young blades of grass that gleam like cut beryl, and with the leaves of kandalī plants newly sprung up, the earth shines with its indragopa insects like a noble lady adorned with jewels that are not white.
t.2.6: Today the flock of peacocks, ever charming, crying out and eager for festivity, made splendid by the peacocks with their broad tails spread wide, and busy with excited embraces and kisses, has begun to dance.
t.2.7: Felling the trees on their banks all around with their muddy waters of swollen force, the rivers rush swiftly toward the ocean, like utterly wanton women whose passions have been stirred.
t.2.8: The forests of the Vindhya captivate the mind, strewn with dark clusters of grass whose tender shoots have sprung up, cropped by the mouths of does, and adorned with trees on which fresh leaves have burst forth.
t.2.9: The sandy woodland tract, thronged on every side with deer whose faces are graced by restless eyes like blue lotuses and in whom alarm has arisen, stirs a deep longing in the heart.
t.2.10: Even on nights made thickly dark by the rain-cloud thundering loudly again and again, women going to meet their lovers set out, driven by passion, the ground of their path revealed by the flashes of lightning.
t.2.11: Their hearts sorely shaken by the clouds with their terrible, deep rumblings and by the lightning flashes, women hold their lovers close in bed without letting go, even those lovers who have wronged them.
t.2.13: The new water, pale and turbid, laden with insects, dust and grass, creeping along in winding courses like a serpent, and watched by troops of frightened frogs, flows on toward the low ground.
t.2.12: With the lovely shoots of their bimba-red lower lips sprinkled by teardrops falling from their blue-lotus eyes, and having cast aside garlands, ornaments and fragrant unguents, the wives of men dwelling far from home remain bereft of hope.
t.2.14: Eager bees, whose humming ravishes the ear, abandon the lotus pond whose flowers have shed their petals and, deluded, fall upon the circling tail-fans of the dancing peacocks in the hope of fresh blue lotuses.
t.2.15: The temples of the wild elephants, filled with rut and trumpeting again and again at the thunder of fresh rain-clouds, shine with the luster of spotless lotuses, covered with streams of rut-fluid swarming with bees.
t.2.16: The mountains, whose rocks are kissed by clouds gleaming like white lotuses, covered on every side with flowing streams and thronged with peacocks that have begun their dance, awaken an eager longing in the heart.
t.2.17: The breeze shakes the groves of kadamba, sarja, arjuna and ketakī, perfumed by their blossoms and cooled by its touch with the spray-laden clouds. Whom does it not fill with longing?
t.2.19: Rivers flow, clouds rain, rutting elephants trumpet, the forest edges shine, those parted from their beloveds pine, peacocks dance, and monkeys take shelter.
t.2.20: The clouds, adorned with creeper-like lightning and Śakra's bow and hanging low under their burden of water, and the women, radiant with girdles, jewels and earrings, together steal the hearts of those who dwell far from home.
t.2.18: With tresses hanging down to the slopes of their hips, with fragrant flowers worn as ornaments, with breasts adorned with necklaces and mouths sweet with wine, women kindle passion in their lovers.
t.2.21: Today women wear on their heads garlands fashioned from fresh kadamba, kesara and ketakī blossoms, and on their ears ornaments made, just as they wish, from clusters of kakubha-tree flowers.
t.2.23: By the clouds, dark as blue lotus petals, towering high and bowed low with water, stirred by gentle breezes and drifting ever so slowly, adorned with rainbows, the hearts of the wives of travelers, distraught at separation from them, are stolen away, as it were.
t.2.22: Their limbs anointed with black aloe-wood and lavish sandalwood, their braided tresses made fragrant with chaplets of flowers, women, hearing the rumble of the clouds at nightfall, hasten from the house of their elders into the bedchamber.
t.2.24: The forest, its heat quenched by the sprinkling of fresh rain, seems delighted with the kadamba trees blossoming on every side, seems to dance with its trees whose branches sway in the wind, and seems to break into laughter with the needle-like buds of the ketakīs.
t.2.25: Like a lover, this season with its massing clouds fashions for young wives a garland of bakula for the head, joined with mālatī blossoms, with freshly opened new flowers and with buds of yūthikā, and an ear-ornament of fresh, full-blown kadambas.
t.2.26: Women bear strings of pearls upon the tips of their lovely, high breasts, fine white silks upon the broad orbs of their hips, and upon their waists, graceful with folds and curves, the line of fine hair that has risen at the sprinkling of fresh raindrops.
t.2.27: Taking on coolness from its contact with fresh raindrops, making the trees bowed under their weight of blossoms dance, and filled with a lovely fragrance from the pollen of the ketakī flowers, the wind steals away the hearts of those who are far from home.
t.2.28: Thinking, “This lofty one is the refuge of us who are bowed down by the weight of water,” the clouds, bent low with water, seem to refresh with showers of water the Vindhya, which had been scorched by the exceedingly harsh flames of summer's fire.
t.2.29: Delightful with its many charms, stealing the hearts of loving women, the steadfast friend of trees, boughs and creepers, this season of clouds, which has become the very breath of life for living beings, may it grant you blessings, and most of all those you desire.
